entry.description: Assigns one character's described attribute to another, or the right attribute at the wrong value.
entry.childHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
entry.approvalNote: Cleared on the printed review pack; returned marked up.

textProvenance.authority: annie-eighteenth-return.md, read from the file, sha256 b2e9e673669861e3b82d8a9a1fbc8a883a9f4b8f634353b3c8b407b74fa468ca

stem.text: Read lines 1 to 4. What had the Mole been doing all morning?

carriers.key: Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.

options.value: Digging out a brand new tunnel.
Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.
Painting his house blue outside and white inside.
options.execution: Blue outside and white within is the Rat's boat at line 60; the colours are carried across to the house.

options.value: Resting his aching back and weary arms.
Singing along with the happy birds.

stem.text: Read lines 3 to 4. What was all over the Mole's black fur?

carriers.key: Splashes of whitewash.

options.value: Dust, which had got into his throat and eyes.
Bits of straw from his brooms.
Warm grass from the great meadow.
Splashes of whitewash.
Blue and white paint.
options.execution: Blue and white are the boat's colours at line 60, transferred onto the fur.

stem.text: Read line 49: 'A grave round face'. What does 'grave' mean here?

carriers.key: Serious and calm.

options.value: Serious and calm.
A place where someone is buried.
Dark and dirty with earth.
options.execution: Earth and dirt belong to the Mole's own fur at line 4, carried across to the Rat's face.

options.value: Very sad and upset.
Round and rather fat.

stem.text: Read line 65. The Mole was 'seated in the stern of a real boat'. What is the stern?

carriers.key: The back part of the boat.

options.value: A strict and serious look.
The oars that push the boat along.
A soft seat with a cushion on it.
The rope that held the boat to the bank.
options.execution: The rope at line 59 is gear ATTACHED to the boat, and this transfers it into being a part OF the boat. The distinction is the item's whole subject, and it is a different error from picking the oars.

options.value: The back part of the boat.

stem.text: The Bennet daughters did not meet Mr Bingley when he called at their house. Read lines 5 to 8. What were they able to find out about him?

carriers.key: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.

options.value: That he was cheerful and talked to everybody.
That he had ten thousand pounds a year.
options.execution: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.
That he stayed about ten minutes with their father.
That he liked the big house he had taken.

stem.text: Mr Bingley hoped for something on this visit that he did not get. Read lines 5 to 6. What was it?

carriers.key: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.

options.value: A book from Mr Bennet's library.
A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.
A chance to invite the Bennets to dinner at his own house.
A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
options.execution: The black horse at line 8 is a thing the ladies saw, turned into something he wanted. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.

options.value: A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet.

stem.text: Mr Bingley said no to the Bennets' dinner. Read lines 9 to 12. What reason did his answer give?

carriers.key: He had to be in London the next day.

options.value: He had promised to dine with Lady Lucas instead.
He did not want to meet the Bennet daughters.
He was busy planning the courses for a dinner of his own.
options.execution: The planning of courses at lines 9 and 10 is MRS BENNET'S, carried across to him.

options.value: He had to be in London the next day.
He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.

stem.text: Mr Bingley's answer upset Mrs Bennet. Read lines 13 to 16. What was she most afraid of?

carriers.key: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.

options.value: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.
That her dinner had all been cooked and would now be wasted.
That he had gone to London to look for guests for the ball.
options.execution: The guest-gathering at lines 16 and 17 is Lady Lucas's comfort, and this transfers it into Mrs Bennet's fear.

options.value: That the girls would have to meet twelve strange ladies.
That Mr Bingley did not like her daughters.

stem.text: When Mr Darcy first walked in, the room thought very well of him. Read lines 26 to 30. Why?

carriers.key: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.

options.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
options.execution: Dancing every dance is Mr Bingley at line 37, carried across to Mr Darcy, who dances twice. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

options.value: Because he spoke kindly to everyone he was introduced to.
Because he was the tallest man in the room.
Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.
Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.

stem.text: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

carriers.key: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He complained that the ball had ended too early.
options.execution: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 31 answers the stem: 'with great admiration for about half the evening, till'.

options.value: Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.

stem.text: Read lines 39 to 41. How many dances did Mr Darcy dance, and who did he dance with?

carriers.key: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.

options.value: Every dance of the evening.
options.execution: Every dance is Mr Bingley's at line 37, one line above, carried across to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 39 answers the stem: 'speak for themselves. What a contrast between him and'.

options.value: Two: one with Mrs Hurst and one with Miss Bingley.
Two: one with Miss Bingley and one with Elizabeth.
None at all.
Three: with Mrs Hurst, Miss Bingley and Miss Bennet.

stem.text: Read lines 6 and 7. Line 7 speaks of 'her attitude and expression'. What does 'attitude' mean here?

carriers.key: The way she was holding herself.

options.value: How tired she was after her journey.
The way she was holding herself.
What she thought about waiting.
How shy and awkward she looked.
options.execution: Gives the girl Matthew's quality; line 6 gives her tense rigidity, not shyness.

stem.text: Who was Matthew expecting to meet at Bright River? (lines 17 and 18)

carriers.key: A boy, sent over by Mrs Spencer.

options.value: A girl, sent over by Mrs Spencer.
options.execution: Keeps the right person but the wrong value: line 17 says he is not expecting a girl.

options.value: A boy, sent over by the man at the station.
His sister Marilla, coming in on the train.
A boy, sent over by Mrs Spencer.

stem.text: Why does Matthew wish Marilla was there? (lines 24 and 25)

carriers.key: He finds this sort of trouble hard to face alone.

options.value: He knows Marilla is the shy one of the two.
options.execution: Gives Marilla the shyness the preamble gives Matthew.

options.value: He finds this sort of trouble hard to face alone.
He hopes Marilla will send the girl straight back.
He wants Marilla to drive the horse home.

stem.text: Read lines 50 to 52. Line 52 says it grew 'darker and darker, stiller and stiller'. Why does the writer write it that way?

carriers.key: To make the change feel slow and steady.

options.value: To show the storm was still getting worse.
To make the change feel slow and steady.
To show Beauty was growing tired at the end of the day.
options.execution: Gives the horse the evening's quality; the lines describe the dark and the quiet.

options.value: To copy the sound of the wheels on the soft road.

stem.text: Beauty says 'I dare not stir'. What does 'stir' mean here? (lines 36 to 38)

carriers.key: Move at all.

options.value: Move at all.
Mix something round and round.
Make any sound.
Wake up from a doze.

stem.text: Lines 1 and 2 speak of 'such a commotion up and down a house'. What does 'commotion' on line 1 mean here?

carriers.key: A great deal of noisy fuss.

options.value: A great deal of noisy fuss.
A long argument between two people.
A slow and careful piece of work.
A crowd of people arriving at once.
options.execution: Moves it to visitors; the people are the family already in the house.

stem.text: Lines 27 to 29 count the helpers as a second, a third, a fourth, a fifth. Why does the writer number them like that?

carriers.key: To make the crowd grow bigger with every word.

options.value: To show the family were well organised.
To show how long the job took to finish.
options.execution: Moves it to time; the numbers count people, and the time is given elsewhere.

options.value: To make the crowd grow bigger with every word.
To help the reader remember all their names.

stem.text: Read lines 20 to 23. What do the children use for the table?

carriers.key: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.

options.value: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.
A baking-tin for salt, and a glass ash-tray for bread.
options.execution: Both objects sit in lines 21 and 22, with their jobs the other way round.

options.value: They find all the right things and lay them out.
Bread and butter, set out ready on the table.

stem.text: Read lines 15 to 17. What do these lines tell you about the trip?

carriers.key: He kept the trip from his mother.

options.value: His mother would have stopped him going.
He had promised Nan he would go out there.
options.execution: Line 15 has him promise a picture, not a visit; the promise moves to the wrong thing.

options.value: His mother told him to go round to Ryan's.
He kept the trip from his mother.

stem.text: The writer moves between tenses by a rule. What decides which he uses?

carriers.key: The present is kept for what is still true, but the walk stays past.

options.value: The walk is two miles out along the sea wall to a ruined cottage.
He tells the whole of it the way his Nan has always told it to them.
Nan's part is in the present, but his own is in the past.
options.execution: Lines 9 and 18 are his own sentences, and both are in the present.

options.value: The present is kept for what is still true, but the walk stays past.

stem.text: Read lines 43 to 46. What do these lines tell you about Tom?

carriers.key: He finished first and watched her, wanting more.

options.value: He did not know that Maggie was looking across at him.
He was pleased to watch her enjoy her half.
He was lost to everything but jam and idleness.
options.execution: That is Maggie at line 46, seesawing on the bough.

options.value: He finished first and watched her, wanting more.

stem.text: Look at lines 10 to 14. What shows us that Ben was in a happy mood?

carriers.key: The way he came hopping and skipping along.

options.value: The calm way of working that is described.
options.execution: Line 10 gives that calm to Tom; this reads it as a sign about Ben.

options.value: The fruit he had in his hand.
The way he came hopping and skipping along.
His heart was light and his hopes were high.

stem.text: Look at lines 34 to 37. How does Ben's feeling about the job change?

carriers.key: He grows more and more taken with it.

options.value: He stops nibbling his apple at last.
He starts to sweep the brush daintily.
options.execution: Lines 34 and 35 give the sweeping to Tom, not to Ben.

options.value: He grows more and more taken with it.
He begins to feel sorry for Tom.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 5. What was the one odd thing about the knocker?

carriers.key: The very great size of the thing itself.

options.value: The very great size of the thing itself.
Scrooge had seen it night and morning.
The thing had hung there for many years.
It had as little fancy about it as any man.
options.execution: Line 3 and line 4 give that want of fancy to Scrooge, not to the knocker.

stem.text: Look at lines 68 to 70. What did the flame do as the ghost came in?

carriers.key: It leaped up and then fell back again.

options.value: It came on through the heavy door.
options.execution: Line 68 gives that to the ghost, not to the flame.

options.value: It leaped up and then fell back again.
It called out that it knew Marley.
Scrooge changed colour as the thing passed.

stem.text: Look at lines 22 to 25. What does 'resignation' on line 22 mean here?

carriers.key: Putting up with something you dislike.

options.value: Putting up with something you dislike.
Giving up a job that you hold.
Sitting in a patient and grave way.
Deciding to laugh along with the rest.
options.execution: Line 23 gives the laughing to some of the others, not to her.

stem.text: Look at lines 26 to 29. Why does Miss Jenkyns send for the other book?

carriers.key: To answer his reading with a reading of her own.

options.value: To show the company that she owns a book-room.
To answer his reading with a reading of her own.
To let the present company judge between the two.
To let the Captain choose the second book.
options.execution: Line 26 has her name the book herself, so this hands her choice to him.

stem.text: Look at lines 52 to 54. What does 'inexorable' on line 53 mean here?

carriers.key: Not to be moved by anything he tried.

options.value: Not able to be excused for what she did.
Still in a fury with him about it.
Not to be moved by anything he tried.
Trying to talk of some pleasanter thing.
options.execution: Lines 52 and 53 give that to the Captain, not to her.

stem.text: Look at lines 8 to 16. How do we know the child was afraid of being late?

carriers.key: She ran to her mother when she was called.

options.value: She had an air of being small for her age.
Her mother counted out the silver with care.
options.execution: Line 16 gives that care to the mother, not to the child.

options.value: She ran to her mother when she was called.
She had been waiting outside since early morning.

stem.text: Look at lines 33 to 35. What does 'oblivion' on line 35 mean here?

carriers.key: Being quite unable to remember.

options.value: Being wiped out altogether.
Being quite unable to remember.
Being lulled by the heat and dust.
Thinking hard about the errands ahead.
options.execution: Line 34 gives the errands as one of the things lulling him, not as his thoughts.

stem.text: Look at lines 45 to 49. What does riding inside stop Rebecca from doing?

carriers.key: The windows only show her bits of things.

options.value: Her trunk has fallen off the back.
The stage is slippery and shiny down there.
Her mother is very choice of the trunk.
options.execution: Line 49 gives that care to her mother, not to her.

options.value: The windows only show her bits of things.

stem.text: Look at lines 53 to 56. What did Rebecca do with her sunshade?

carriers.key: Put it under the folds of her dress.

options.value: Pushed it back off her head.
options.execution: Line 55 gives that to her hat, not to the sunshade.

options.value: Put it under the folds of her dress.
Smoothed it out with great care.
Held it up against the afternoon sun.

stem.text: Look at lines 19 and 20. What does "yielding" on line 20 mean here?

carriers.key: Soft, so that a foot sinks into it.

options.value: Soft, so that a foot sinks into it.
Giving in to somebody who insists.
Marked with the prints of somebody who has walked over it.
Moving slowly and stubbornly along.
options.execution: Line 19's manner belongs to Bevis, not to the sand.

stem.text: Look at lines 21 to 25. What does Heidi keep sobbing out?

carriers.key: That the bread was all for grandmother and is gone.

options.value: That her heart would break.
That the bread was all for grandmother and is gone.
That she is distressed and alarmed.
options.execution: True at lines 25 and 26, and it belongs to Clara.

options.value: That she wants to go back to the mountain.

stem.text: Look at lines 28 to 30. What does he tell his mum?

carriers.key: That he does not want a go up front.

options.value: That she asked him about going up front.
That it is all right then, love.
options.execution: True at line 30, and the words belong to his mother.

options.value: That he does not want a go up front.
That the others would not let him go up front.

stem.text: Look at lines 14 to 16. What did the big man say about Rikki-tikki?

carriers.key: That he was not dead, only half choked.

options.value: That he was dead when they carried him in.
That he opened his eyes and sneezed.
That he was not dead, only half choked.
That they might take him in and dry him.
options.execution: Line 13 gives those words to the mother, and line 14 has them already indoors.

stem.text: Look at lines 25 to 28. What does Dilan say about Reception?

carriers.key: They are fine, and the screaming is just what Reception is like.

options.value: That seven of the butterflies are back.
They had to sit down and have a drink of water.
options.execution: True at line 25, and it belongs to Miss Deller, not Reception.

options.value: They are fine, and the screaming is just what Reception is like.
Their teacher took the whole class outside.

stem.text: Look at lines 2 to 5. What did Amy do while the others answered Jo?

carriers.key: She poked the fire and said nothing.

options.value: She poked the fire and said nothing.
She said no at once and looked surprised.
options.execution: True at line 4, and it belongs to Meg and Beth.

options.value: Her colour rose while Jo was watching her.
She went red and owned up straight away.

stem.text: Look at lines 28 to 30. What did Meg and Beth each do?

carriers.key: Meg went to Amy and Beth went to Jo.

options.value: Meg went to Amy and Beth went to Jo.
Meg went to Jo and Beth went to Amy.
options.execution: True of line 28 with the two of them swapped.

options.value: One of them boxed her sister’s ear.
They went up to the garret after her.

stem.text: Look at lines 64 to 66. What did Jo do while Amy put her skates on?

carriers.key: She went slowly down the river without turning.

options.value: She stamped her feet and blew on her fingers.
options.execution: True at lines 64 and 65, and it is Amy rather than Jo.

options.value: She saw Amy coming and turned her back on her.
She went slowly down the river without turning.
She called out to Amy to hurry along after her.

stem.text: Look at lines 25 to 29. What does Grandad answer when Alan mentions Thursday?

carriers.key: If I’m about.

options.value: You’ll be about.
options.execution: True at line 29, and the words are Alan’s.

options.value: That Alan brought a marrow he did not want.
That he will get the beans in himself.
If I’m about.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 4. Setting modesty aside, what does the narrator admit?

carriers.key: That he made a very fine figure.

options.value: That he made a very fine figure.
That he was dressed all in white but his boots.
That he would be doing the King little credit.
options.execution: True at line 3, and it belongs to what he says of the King.

options.value: That he had been practising the ride for days.

stem.text: Look at lines 64 to 68. Why is the narrator thankful about old Lord Topham?

carriers.key: Because the old man could hardly see.

options.value: Because he had danced at Lord Topham’s house many times.
Because the ambassadors had paid their respects.
options.execution: True at line 65, and it belongs to the ambassadors as a group.

options.value: Because the old man could hardly see.
Because the old man had left before he arrived.
